title: Onsets & Rimes
keyIdea: A one-syllable word splits into an onset and a rime. The onset is the sound or sounds before the vowel, and the rime is the vowel and everything after it: c + at = cat, sh + ip = ship, fr + og = frog. Blending puts them together to say the word, and segmenting splits it apart. In a CVC word each letter is one sound, so you can find the first, middle and last sound, and change just one sound to make a new word, like cat to bat.

kid: Words have parts. In cat, the first part is c. That is the onset. The rest is at. That is the rime.
Push them together and say it fast: c, at, cat! That is blending. Now swap the onset. h, at, hat. m, at, mat. Same rime, new word.
The rime starts at the vowel. In ship, s and h make one sound, sh. So ship is sh and ip. In frog, f and r go first. So frog is fr and og.
Say dog slowly: d, o, g. d is the first sound, o is the middle, g is the last. Change one sound and you get a new word. Change d to l and dog is log.
adult: This is phonics and phonological awareness for ages 4 to 7. In England it sits in the Reception and Year 1 word reading work: children blend phonemes to read words and segment them to spell. In the US, Common Core RF.K.2 asks children to blend and segment onsets and rimes of one-syllable words, isolate the initial, medial vowel and final phonemes in CVC words, and add or substitute phonemes to make new words.

Key terms: a phoneme is one sound; a grapheme is the letter or letters that write it. The onset is the consonant sound or sounds before the vowel; the rime is the vowel and what follows. A digraph such as sh or ch is two letters for one phoneme, so it is one onset sound. A blend such as fr or st is two phonemes said quickly, and both belong to the onset. Words that share a rime, like bug, mug and hug, form a word family.

Common mistakes: putting the vowel in the onset (do + g), splitting a digraph (s + hip), saying the letter name instead of the sound, and adding an uh sound to stop sounds (cuh-at), which makes blending harder. Be careful with the middle sound: children often say the last sound they heard. Ask them to say the word slowly and tap a finger for each sound.

In the lab your child pushes an onset tile onto a rime and picks the matching picture, builds bug, mug and hug from pictures, cuts dog, ship and frog into onset and rime, taps the first, middle or last sound in a CVC word, and swaps one letter to make bat, cap and pen. Vowel tiles are pink with a dot so the start of the rime is easy to see.

familyTip: Play I spy with rimes: 'I spy something that ends in -at… it starts with h.' Then swap: 'Now change the h to c. What is it?' Keep the sounds short: say c, not cuh.

visual.caption: Which word family? Drag each word, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: blend onset and rime, build a word family, cut words at the vowel, find first, middle and last sounds, and swap one sound to make a new word.

practice.prompt: Onsets & Rimes: in the word ship, what is the onset?
practice.hint: The onset is every sound before the vowel. Is sh one sound or two?
practice.explain: s and h together make one sound, sh. It comes before the vowel i, so the onset is sh and the rime is ip.

practice.prompt: You make {n} words in the -ug family, like bug and mug. Each one is a CVC word with 3 sounds. How many sounds do you say in all?
practice.hint: Each word has a first, a middle and a last sound. Count 3 for every word.
practice.explain: 3 sounds in each word, and {n} words, is {=3*n} sounds. The middle and last sounds are the same each time: u, g.

practice.prompt: Change the first sound in dog to l. What new word do you make?
practice.hint: Only the first sound changes. Keep o and g the same.
practice.explain: Swap d for l and keep og: l + og = log.

practice.prompt: Every one-syllable word splits into 2 parts: an onset and a rime. You split {n} words. How many parts is that?
practice.hint: Each word gives you 2 parts. Count 2 for each word.
practice.explain: 2 parts for each of {n} words makes {=2*n} parts: {n} onsets and {n} rimes.

pool.prompt: What is the rime in frog?
pool.hint: The rime starts at the vowel. Find the vowel first.
pool.explain: f and r blend together as the onset, fr. The rime is the vowel and what follows: og.

pool.prompt: Blend s + un. What word is it?
pool.hint: Say the onset first, then the rime, quickly: s, un.
pool.explain: s first, then un, said fast together, makes sun.

pool.prompt: The -at family has cat, hat and mat. You add {n} more -at words, like sat and bat. How many -at words is that now?
pool.hint: Start at 3 for cat, hat and mat, then count on.
pool.explain: 3 words and {n} more makes {=3+n} words, all with the same rime, at.

pool.prompt: What is the middle sound in pen?
pool.hint: Say it slowly: p, e, n. Which sound is between the other two?
pool.explain: p is first, e is in the middle and n is last. The middle sound is e.

pool.prompt: Which word is in the same word family as hug?
pool.hint: A word family shares the same rime. What is the rime in hug?
pool.explain: hug has the rime ug, and so does mug. hat starts like hug, but its rime is at; bag has the rime ag. So only mug is in the -ug family.

pool.prompt: A CVC word has 3 sounds. You change 1 sound in each of {n} words to make new words. How many sounds stay the same?
pool.hint: In each word, 1 sound changes and the other 2 stay.
pool.explain: 2 sounds stay in each word, and {n} words, makes {=2*n} sounds that stay the same.

pool.prompt: Change the last sound in cat to p. What word is it?
pool.hint: Only the last sound changes. Keep c and a.
pool.explain: Keep c and a, and change t to p: cap.

pool.prompt: How do you split chin into onset and rime?
pool.hint: c and h make one sound here. The rime starts at the vowel i.
pool.explain: ch is one sound, a digraph, and it comes before the vowel. So chin is ch + in.
